title: Compass Bench
context: Grade 4, and the chapter's longest run of exercises. An adult sees a circle being drawn and its parts named. What is actually being settled is that every point of a circle is the same distance from its centre, which is why a pair of compasses works at all, and that a diameter is simply two radii end to end. The page's summary box says every chord is not a diameter, meaning that not every chord is a diameter; as printed it says no chord is one, which contradicts the diameter drawn beside it.

writeup.why: Draw a circle with a pair of compasses, name what joins its centre and its edge, and find out why a diameter is two radii long.
writeup.look: A pair of compasses standing on a sheet of paper, a parts tray beside it, and a chord slider and a radius bar along the foot of the canvas.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Compass Bench' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the circles drawn and the parts named against what this phase lays out, two numbers in ink, the first climbing by one as each circle closes or each part takes its tag, and the second fixed at what this phase holds. The chord's length, which rises and falls as it slides, is read in its own box and never here. Nothing in it ever counts down and nothing in it ever reads as a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. The sheet fills the left of the working area, 640 by 470 at 64,214, on the panel colour, and the pair of compasses stands on it, a metal point on one arm and a pencil on the other, with a near-black ruler drawn along the pencil arm. Pressed into the paper, the metal point drops a vermilion dot that takes a capital letter as the centre. The pencil arm stretches to a length read off the ruler, and the turn control moves the pencil round the fixed point, drawing the circle in deep blue while an amber string runs from the centre to the pencil and never changes length. Stretching the arm wider and turning again draws a bigger circle about the same centre, so rings on one centre can be stacked, the largest 460 across. The chord slider is an upright rail, 40 by 470 at 716,214, beside the sheet: its handle moves a level chord up and down across the circle, drawn sky blue while it misses the centre. As it passes exactly through the centre dot it turns deep blue, the word diameter lights under it, and its length is at its greatest there. The parts tray stands at the right, 380 by 150 at 770,214, with name tags for centre, radius, chord, diameter and circumference, and it names a segment the child draws by where its two ends lie: one end on the centre dot and one on the circle is a radius, both on the circle is a chord, and both on the circle with the segment passing through the centre is a diameter, which the tray also names a chord. Every radius of one circle lights at the same length when any one of them is measured. The double and halve slot stands under the tray, 380 by 130 at 770,380, and the radius bar under that, 380 by 90 at 770,526: the bar lays a second radius end to end with the first through the centre, and the slot turns a radius into a diameter or a diameter into a radius, showing the two radii each time. The chord's length is read in a box under the bar, 380 by 60 at 770,632. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve number keys three across wherever a length is asked for, with a unit tag under the slot that is filled in with the number, and a word pad wherever a part is named, with keys reading centre, radius, chord, diameter, circumference and concentric circles. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own and are the pictures' colours too. The figure being studied, every line, segment, ray, side, outline, circle, angle arm and visible edge of a solid, is deep blue. Every point, end point, corner dot, vertex dot and the centre dot of a circle is vermilion. A length being measured, walked, added or named, and every angle arc and square corner mark, is amber. The unit squares that cover an area, the flood inside a closed figure and a face of a solid being counted are green. A line of symmetry or a mirror line is reddish purple and always dotted. The second thing set beside the first, a fold being tried, a mirror image, the other half of a fold, a chord that is not a diameter and the larger angle between clock hands, is sky blue. A hidden edge of a solid is grey and dashed, and grey is used for nothing else. Chrome never borrows one of those and none of them is ever used for chrome: every grid line, ruler tick, bracket, guide line and table rule is near-black. Every reading survives with the colour taken away, because a point is a round dot, a line carries an arrowhead at each end, a ray a dot and one arrowhead and a segment a dot at each end, a measured length carries its number, a hidden edge is dashed and a line of symmetry is dotted, before any of them is told by a colour. A dotted line always means a true line of symmetry or a mirror line, and a fold being tried is drawn solid until it is kept, so nothing else on any stage of this chapter is ever dotted. The centre dot is drawn on every circle that shows its parts, every radius runs from that dot, and a diameter always passes exactly through it. No letter names two things on this sheet: a point named as the end of a diameter is never renamed as a centre, and a segment named as a diameter is never renamed as a radius.
writeup.finish: The card shows the circle the child drew with its centre named, its radius, a chord and a diameter labelled, and the two radii lying end to end.

phases.win: the circle closes, the string from the centre holds one length all the way round, and a wider circle forms about the same centre
phases.does: fixes the metal point, stretches the pencil arm, turns it round, then stretches wider and turns again
phases.goal: every point of a circle is the same distance from its centre, and the length of the boundary is the circumference
phases.says: Fix the point and turn the pencil round it. Is the string the same all the way?
phases.check: Away from the screen: draw two circles about one centre with a pair of compasses, the second wider. Mark the centre. What do the two circles share?
phases.feels: the string never changes length, so every point of the curve is the same distance from the centre
phases.hands: Tie a length of string to a peg, or to a child standing still, and walk round with a piece of chalk held at the string's end, keeping the string tight. Ask why the chalk line closes up. Then let more string out and walk again round the same centre, and ask what the two circles share.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the answer. First rung, from the item's own miss line: where is the metal point fixed? Second rung, the phase's: does the string change length as the pencil turns? Third rung: the arm is set to a short opening and turned once slowly with the string drawn, before the larger circle comes back. The word pad stays open behind all three rungs.

wrong.why: a circle is judged by how wide it looks, and arms spread apart look like a width.
wrong.move: takes the opening of the compass arms as the distance right across the circle, and draws a circle twice as wide as the one asked for.
wrong.screen: the circle is drawn at the child's opening and a ruler is laid across it through the centre dot: it reads twice the opening. The string from the centre to the pencil is drawn at the same time, reading the opening itself, and both readings stay beside the child's answer, nothing marked.

wrong.why: the pencil arm is the one doing the drawing, so the hand watches it and lets the other arm wander.
wrong.move: lets the metal point slide while turning, so the curve does not close up where it began.
wrong.screen: the curve is drawn as the child turned it, with the amber string drawn from wherever the metal point stood at each moment, changing length as it goes, and the curve misses its own beginning. The metal point is then pinned and the turn made again, the string holding one length all the way round, and the circle closes exactly. Both curves stay drawn.

phases.screen: a pair of compasses on a blank sheet with its metal point raised
phases.soWhat: Every point of a circle is the same distance from its centre, and the length of the boundary is the circumference.
phases.concept: The same distance all the way round

phases.win: the tray names the radius and the chord, and every other radius drawn lights at the same length
phases.does: draws one segment from the centre to the circle and one between two points on the circle, and names each
phases.goal: a radius joins the centre to the circle and a chord joins two points on the circle
phases.says: One starts at the centre and one does not. Which is the radius?
phases.check: Draw a circle and name its centre O. Draw three radii and two chords, and name each one.
phases.feels: a radius always has one end on the centre dot, and a chord never needs it
phases.hands: Draw a big circle on the board with its centre marked and named. Ask one child to draw a segment from the centre to the circle, and another to join two points on the circle. Measure every segment the class draws from the centre and ask what they all share. Then measure two chords and compare them.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: where does the segment start? Second rung, the phase's: is either end at the centre? Third rung: the circle is cut to one radius and one chord drawn far apart, and each end is lit in turn. The word pad stays open.

wrong.why: radius is the first name met for a segment inside a circle, so it stretches to cover all of them.
wrong.move: calls a segment joining two points on the circle a radius, because it lies inside the circle.
wrong.screen: the parts tray lights the centre dot and then the two ends of the child's segment: both glow on the curve and neither is at the centre, and the tray writes chord under it. A true radius is drawn from the centre dot beside it, and the child's name stays in the slot, nothing marked.

wrong.why: near the middle looks like the middle, and the centre dot is small.
wrong.move: draws a radius from a point near the middle of the circle rather than from the centre dot itself.
wrong.screen: the child's segment is measured, and so is a radius drawn from the centre dot to the same place on the curve; the two lengths differ. Three more radii are drawn from the dot and all light at one length, which the child's segment does not match, and every segment stays drawn.

phases.screen: a circle with its centre named and the parts tray waiting
phases.soWhat: A radius joins the centre to the circle, and every radius of one circle is the same length; a chord joins two points on the circle.

phases.win: the chord lights as a diameter as it crosses the centre, and its length reading peaks there
phases.does: slides the chord across the circle, reading its length, and stops where it passes through the centre
phases.goal: a chord through the centre is a diameter and the longest chord, and not every chord is a diameter
phases.says: Slide the chord across. Where is it longest? What is it called there?
phases.check: Draw a circle and three chords, one of them through the centre. Which is the diameter? Which chord is longest?
phases.feels: the chord grows as it slides towards the centre, and is longest exactly there, where it becomes a diameter
phases.hands: Draw a circle and several chords across it, one of them through the centre. Measure them all and write each length on its chord. Ask which is longest and what is special about where it runs. Then say both halves of the rule: every diameter is a chord, but not every chord is a diameter.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: does the chord pass through the centre dot? Second rung, the phase's: where is its length greatest as it slides? Third rung: the slider is set just off the centre, and the child moves it one step at a time until it lights. The word pad and the number pad stay open.

wrong.why: the diameter is the long one, and a chord almost as long looks as though it must be it.
wrong.move: calls a long chord that just misses the centre a diameter.
wrong.screen: the slider holds the child's chord where it is, with its length in the box, then slides it the last small step until it passes through the centre dot. It lights as a diameter only there, and its length climbs a little higher. Slid back, it loses the light and its length drops, and the child's chord stays drawn in sky blue beside the diameter, nothing marked.

wrong.why: a part with its own name sounds like a different kind of thing, and the summary box on circles prints its rule with the not in the wrong place, so that read as printed it says no chord is a diameter; what it means is that not every chord is a diameter.
wrong.move: decides that no chord can be a diameter, because a diameter has a name of its own.
wrong.screen: the diameter is drawn through the centre dot and its two ends light on the curve, where every chord has its ends, and the parts tray writes chord under it as well as diameter. A chord that misses the centre is drawn beside it with the one name only, and the rule is written under both: every diameter is a chord, and not every chord is a diameter.

phases.screen: a circle with a chord near its edge and the chord slider waiting
phases.soWhat: A chord through the centre is a diameter and the longest chord. Every diameter is a chord, but not every chord is a diameter.

phases.win: the two radii span the circle as a diameter, and the slot doubles the radius and halves the diameter back
phases.does: lays a second radius end to end with the first through the centre, then uses the slot both ways
phases.goal: a diameter is two radii end to end, so it is twice the radius, and the radius is half the diameter
phases.says: Lay two radii end to end through the centre. What have you made?
phases.check: A round table top has a radius of forty-five centimetres. How long is its diameter? A coin is two centimetres across. What is its radius?
phases.feels: a diameter is just a radius on each side of the centre, laid end to end
phases.hands: Cut a strip of card as long as a circle's radius, hold one end at the centre and swing it round. Lay a second strip of the same length on the other side of the centre, in a straight line with the first. Ask how far the two reach across the circle together, and what that length is called.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: is the radius or the diameter given? Second rung, the phase's: how many radii fit across the circle through the centre? Third rung: the circle is cut to a radius of one, and the radius bar lays two end to end before the larger circle comes back. The number pad stays open.

wrong.why: the radius and the diameter are learnt as a pair with a two between them, and which way the two goes is easy to lose.
wrong.move: halves the radius instead of doubling it, writing three for the diameter of a circle of radius six.
wrong.screen: the radius bar lays a second radius of six end to end with the first through the centre, and together they reach from the circle across to the circle, twelve. The child's three is drawn as a bar from the centre, reaching only half way to the curve, and both stay drawn, nothing marked.

wrong.why: doubling has just been the step that worked, and the question's numbers look just like the last ones.
wrong.move: doubles a diameter when the radius is asked for, giving a plate twenty-four centimetres across a radius of forty-eight.
wrong.screen: the plate's diameter is laid across it through the centre and the slot halves it into two radii that meet at the centre dot, twelve each. The child's forty-eight is drawn as a bar from the centre, running far past the rim, and both stay drawn, nothing marked.

phases.screen: a circle with one radius drawn and measured, and the radius bar waiting
phases.soWhat: The diameter is twice the radius, and the radius is half the diameter.

writeup.delight: The third phase, the moment the sliding chord reaches the centre dot. The sky blue chord has been growing longer as it slides, its length climbing in the box, and as it touches the dot it turns deep blue and the word diameter lights under it; slide it one step on and it turns sky blue again and starts to shrink. The length in the box is at its greatest exactly while the chord is lit. It can be slid back and forth across the dot as often as a finger likes, nothing is marked, and the voice says nothing at all while it happens.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. On the first phase the pair of compasses stands on a blank sheet with its metal point raised just above the paper and its pencil arm closed. On the second a circle is already drawn with its centre dot named, and the parts tray lies open and empty beside it. On the third a circle stands with one chord drawn near its rim and the handle of the chord slider resting level with that chord, its length read in the box beside it. On the fourth a circle stands with one radius drawn and measured, the radius bar folded under it and the double and halve slot empty. The running count at the top left holds the circles drawn or the parts named against what this phase lays out, and the answer slot and the pad stand empty down the right. One thing moves, once: the metal point, or the centre dot, or the slider's handle, or the measured radius, gives one slow pulse while the voice asks where the centre will be. That pulse is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any circle, any number of radii and chords, circles stacked on one centre, and the chord slider and the radius bar open. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on the centre and the circumference, radii and chords, the chord through the centre, and doubling and halving between radius and diameter.

A new circle. Find its centre before you name anything.
Free play. Any circle, any opening, rings on one centre, with the slider and the bar open.

Every circle drawn round a fixed point, every part named, and every diameter two radii long.

observations.why: The metal point stayed fixed and the arm did not change, so the pencil was always the same distance away.
observations.soWhat: Every point of a circle is the same distance from its centre, which is why a pair of compasses draws one.
observations.observe: The string from the centre to the pencil held one length all the way round.

observations.why: Every radius runs from the centre to the circle, while a chord can join any two points on the circle.
observations.soWhat: A circle has many radii, all the same length, and many chords, which can have different lengths.
observations.observe: Every radius drawn lit at the same length, and the chords did not.

observations.why: A chord is longest when it runs right through the middle of the circle.
observations.soWhat: Every diameter is a chord, but not every chord is a diameter, and the diameter is the longest chord.
observations.observe: The chord lit as a diameter only as it crossed the centre, and its length was greatest there.

observations.why: A diameter runs from the circle to the centre and on to the circle again, one radius each side.
observations.soWhat: The diameter is twice the radius, and the radius is half the diameter.
observations.observe: Two radii laid end to end through the centre reached exactly across the circle.

source_tool.description: A pair of compasses stands on a sheet of paper. Its metal point is pressed into the paper to fix the centre, its pencil arm is stretched to a length read off a ruler along the arm, and turning the pencil arm round draws a circle. A string from the centre to the pencil stays the same length all the way round, and stretching the arm wider draws a bigger circle about the same centre, so circles with one centre and different radii can be stacked. A parts tray names what the child draws: a segment from the centre to the circle is named a radius, and a segment joining two points on the circle is named a chord. A chord slider moves a chord across the circle, reading its length as it goes, and lights it as a diameter at the one place where it passes through the centre, where its length is greatest. A radius bar lays two radii end to end through the centre so that together they span the circle, and a doubling and halving slot turns a radius into a diameter and a diameter into a radius.
source_tool.art_direction: Compasses turning on a sheet of paper / Picture book

modes.freePlay: Out of scope here. It is not reached from inside a phase mount, because a phase mount ends idle and has no finish card to reach it from. writeup.freePlay stays as the record of what that activity is, for whoever builds it as its own thing.

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: a drawing board with a ruler and a point stamp, a tracing finger and a flag, a walker and a string, square tiles on squared paper, a pair of compasses with a metal point and a pencil arm, a sheet of paper that folds, an upright mirror, solids on a turntable, flat nets that fold up, hinged arms, a clock face and a grid of pictures.

A line is always drawn with an arrowhead at each end, a ray with a dot at its end point and one arrowhead, and a line segment with a dot at each end. No stroke is ever left with a bare end that could be read as either.

A point is drawn as one small dot of one size wherever it appears, named by a capital letter beside it. Within one figure no letter ever names two different things, and a figure never renames a part it has already named.

Every labelled length is one the figure could really have, and every figure is drawn to scale with its labels. A triangle drawn with a square corner carries lengths such as three, four and five, and a stepped shape's sides close up exactly.
A figure on squared paper sits exactly on the grid lines, with every side along a line and every square either wholly inside it or wholly outside it.

A circle drawn to show its parts has its centre marked as a dot and named. Every radius is drawn from that dot to the curve, and a diameter always passes exactly through the dot. A circle that is a view of a solid carries a dot only where the solid has a point, so a cylinder seen from above is a plain circle.
A right angle carries a small square corner mark, and every other angle an arc drawn close to its vertex between the arms.

A line of symmetry and a mirror line are drawn dotted and lie exactly where the fold falls. A fold line being tried is drawn solid and turns dotted only once the fold is kept. Every mirror line stands upright unless the frame says it lies across, and an image sits exactly as far behind the line as the thing in front of it, turned the other way round.
A solid is drawn with its hidden edges dashed. Views of one solid are drawn at one scale, so the front view and the side view of a box are exactly the same height.

Clock hands point exactly at the numbers and the minute hand is the longer. Where the angle between the hands is shown, both angles are shaded and the smaller one is outlined. No clock is set to six o'clock or twelve o'clock.
A grid carries its row numbers down the left edge and its column numbers across the top, and each picture in it appears once.
A shape, a side or a part is told apart by its label first and by its colour second, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a line, a point, a square or a part the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. These are the chapter's own colours, taken from the pictures, so a tool and a picture of the same thing are the same colour. The figure being studied, every line, segment, ray, side, outline, circle, angle arm and visible edge of a solid, is deep blue. Every point, end point, corner dot, vertex dot and the centre dot of a circle is vermilion, in every tool without exception, because a chapter that opens on the point cannot afford a frame where a point has to be hunted for. A length being measured, walked, added or named, the tape, the walker's sum, a radius being measured, and every angle arc and square corner mark, is amber. The unit squares that cover an area, the flood inside a closed figure and a face of a solid being counted are green. A line of symmetry or a mirror line is reddish purple and always dotted, so a dotted line always means a true line of symmetry. Sky blue is the second thing set beside the first: a fold being tried, drawn solid until it is kept, a mirror image, the other half of a fold, a chord that is not a diameter, and the larger angle between clock hands. A hidden edge of a solid is grey and dashed, and grey is used for nothing else. Every grid line, ruler tick, bracket, guide line and table rule is near-black chrome. All of that holds in greyscale, because a point is a round dot, a measured length carries its number, a line of symmetry is dotted, a fold being tried is solid and a hidden edge is dashed.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Put a finger on the centre dot, and follow the segment from there.
voice.onNext: A new circle. Find its centre before you name anything.
voice.opening: A pair of compasses on a clean sheet. Where will the centre of your circle be?
voice.onFinish: Every circle drawn round a fixed point, every part named, and every diameter two radii long.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Any circle, any opening, rings on one centre, with the slider and the bar open.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.

phase_map.concept: The same distance all the way round

placement.where: After a circle has been drawn on the ground with a string held tight at its centre, and before any circle is named. The tool is what holds the compass arm at one length while it turns, and lights a chord as a diameter at the one place it passes through the centre, which a drawing cannot show happening.

answer_key.rule: Every point of a circle is the same distance from a fixed point, its centre, and a circle is named by its centre. The length of its boundary is its circumference. A segment joining the centre to a point on the circle is a radius, and every radius of one circle has the same length. A segment joining two points on the circle is a chord, and chords can have different lengths. A chord through the centre is a diameter, every diameter of one circle has the same length, and the diameter is the longest chord. Every diameter is a chord, but not every chord is a diameter. A diameter is a radius on each side of the centre, so the diameter is twice the radius and the radius is half the diameter. A circle has many radii, chords and diameters but only one centre. Circles with the same centre and different radii are concentric circles.
answer_key.wrong: The compass arm is turned again slowly with the string from the centre drawn in, and the chord slider is run back across the centre so the change in its length is seen. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: The metal point stays fixed at K while the pencil arm turns round it.
The arm does not change length, so the pencil is always three centimetres from K.
So every point of the circle is three centimetres from K, and K is its centre.
items.answer: Three centimetres; K is the centre of the circle
items.question: The metal point of a pair of compasses is fixed at point K, and the pencil arm is opened to three centimetres. How far from K is every point of the circle drawn?
items.checkpoint: Every point of a circle is the same distance from its centre.
items.misconception: Thinking the opening of the arms is the distance right across the circle rather than from its centre.

steps: A radius joins the centre to a point on the circle, and OA starts at the centre O.
A chord joins two points on the circle, and B and C both lie on the circle.
So OA is a radius and BC is a chord, and a circle has many of each.
items.answer: OA is a radius, and BC is a chord
items.question: In circle O, segment OA joins the centre to the circle, and segment BC joins two points on the circle without passing through O. Name the radius and the chord.
items.checkpoint: A radius joins the centre to the circle; a chord joins two points on the circle.
items.misconception: Calling any segment inside a circle a radius, whether or not it starts at the centre.

steps: A diameter is a chord that passes through the centre, and DE passes through O.
FG is still a chord, because it joins two points on the circle, but it misses the centre.
The diameter is the longest chord in a circle, so DE is longer than FG; not every chord is a diameter.
items.answer: DE is a diameter, and it is longer than FG. FG is a chord but not a diameter
items.question: In circle O, chord DE passes through O and chord FG does not. Which is a diameter, and which is longer?
items.checkpoint: Every diameter is a chord, but not every chord is a diameter, and the diameter is the longest chord.
items.misconception: Thinking a chord and a diameter are different kinds of thing, so that a diameter cannot be a chord.

steps: A diameter runs from the circle through the centre to the circle again.
So it is one radius on each side of the centre, laid end to end.
Six and six make twelve, so the diameter is twelve centimetres, twice the radius.
items.question: A circle has a radius of six centimetres. How long is its diameter?
items.checkpoint: The diameter is twice the radius, and the radius is half the diameter.
items.misconception: Halving the radius instead of doubling it, and giving three centimetres.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: What is the length of the boundary of a circle called?
Four circles are drawn about one centre, the pencil arm opened wider each time. What are circles with one centre and different radii called?
In circle P, segment PQ joins the centre to the circle. What is PQ, and how does its length compare with another radius, PR?
items.final_answer: PQ is a radius, and it is the same length as PR, because every radius of one circle is equal

items.question: Name three parts that a circle has many of, and one part it has only one of.
items.final_answer: Many radii, chords and diameters, and only one centre

items.question: Is every diameter a chord? Is every chord a diameter?
items.final_answer: Every diameter is a chord, because it joins two points on the circle. But not every chord is a diameter; only a chord through the centre is

items.question: In a circle, the diameter is eight centimetres. Could a chord of that circle be ten centimetres long?
items.final_answer: No. The diameter is the longest chord, so no chord can be longer than eight centimetres

items.question: A round clock face has a diameter of twenty-eight centimetres. What is its radius?
A round pond has a radius of thirty-five metres. What is its diameter?
items.final_answer: Seventy metres, because the diameter is two radii end to end

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

student_controls.effect: fixes the centre where it is pressed into the paper
stretches to a length read off the ruler along the arm
draws the circle by moving the pencil arm round the fixed point
shows the distance from the centre to the pencil staying the same all the way round
names a drawn segment as a radius or a chord
moves a chord across the circle, reading its length, and lights it as a diameter at the centre
lays two radii end to end through the centre
turns a radius into a diameter and a diameter into a radius

teaching_notes: Draw a circle on the ground first, with a string held tight by a child standing at the centre. The string is a radius, and walking round with it pulled tight is the whole reason every point is the same distance away. The compass steps on the page are fix the point, stretch the arm, turn the pencil; say them in that order. The summary box says every diameter is a chord, but every chord is not a diameter. It means not every chord is a diameter, and as printed it says the opposite of its own first half, so say the corrected form and never the printed one. The labelled circle on the page calls one segment a diameter in one figure and a radius in the next; keep one name for one thing in every figure drawn here. One printed blank, a circle can have many, has three right answers, radii, chords and diameters, so accept any of them. The Math Lab stacks four circles on one centre, which is where the word concentric comes from. Its last step suggests pencils as darts, and this plan leaves that step out: stick the rings on the board and name them instead.
generation_prompt: Build a circle tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. A pair of compasses stands on a sheet in the working area, with a metal point on one arm and a pencil on the other. The metal point is pressed into the paper to fix the centre, which is drawn as a dot and named with a capital letter. The pencil arm stretches to a length read off a ruler drawn along the arm, and a turn control moves the pencil round the fixed point, drawing the circle; a thin string from the centre to the pencil stays drawn during the turn, and its length never changes. Stretching the arm wider and turning again draws a bigger circle about the same centre. A parts tray names a segment the child draws from the centre to the circle as a radius and one joining two points on the circle as a chord, and every radius of one circle lights at the same length. A chord slider moves a chord across the circle with its length read out as it goes, and lights it as a diameter only as it passes exactly through the centre, where the reading peaks. A radius bar lays a second radius end to end with the first through the centre, and a slot doubles a radius into a diameter or halves a diameter into a radius. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Fix the metal point. Stretch the pencil arm and turn it round. Name the centre. A radius starts at the centre. A chord joins two points on the circle. A diameter is a chord through the centre.
